To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the N-terminus of the β-cyanobacterial protein CcmM, previously thought to be an uncharacterized carboxysomal structural protein, has been shown to be a functional, zinc-dependent γ-carbonic anydrase that is active as a trimeric enzyme, and that the structure of Ccm209, the active form, is similar to that of the γ-carbonic hydrase Cam, except that Ccm209 has an additional α-helix that stabilizes

the cyanobacterial carboxysomal CcmM protein is the first bacterial γ-carbonic acid hydrase, that the CcmM protein has a unique disulfide bond that is required for activity and that the carboxysomes are oxidizing microcompartments.
the N-terminal domain of CcmM from β-cyanobacterial carboxysomes has CA activity, and the enzyme is activated by oxidizing conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis for the oxidative activation of CcmM.
elucidating the structure and mechanism of the cyanobacterial carboxysomal carbonic anhydrases.
understanding the structural basis of the oxidative inactivation of CcmM, a key component of the cyanobacterial carboxysome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the β-carboxy-some is a microcompartment that maintains an oxidizing environment by excluding reducing agents.
the CcmM209 protein is the first bacterial γ-CA that has been characterized and shown to have CA activity.
the carboxysomes of T. elongatus are able to maintain an oxidative environment by excluding the thioredoxins and other endogenous reductants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the β-carboxy-some is an oxidative compartment that requires an oxidized CcmM209 to be active as a CA.
CcmM is a γ-CA whose activity can be regulated in vivo by the cellular redox state.
CcmM209 has a structure similar to Cam and is a functional γ-CA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CcmM is the first catalytically functional bacterial γ-CA and that the C-terminal region of the protein is critical to maintaining its oxidized and active state.
CcmM is an active, but inactive, γ-CA in vivo and that the carboxysomes of β-cyanobacterial strains lacking CcaA are able to maintain an oxidative environment to keep CcmM active as a CA.
CcmM, a protein that was previously thought to be inactive in the β-carboxy-some, is actually an active enzyme in the interior of this compartment.
